lessons.title: Common Alpha Factors: Value, Momentum, and Mean-Reversion Signals

children.text: Lesson 25 introduced the factor families briefly: value, momentum, quality, size, and the relative-value and mean-reversion family this course has been building all along. This lesson goes deeper on three of them, value, momentum, and mean-reversion, and resolves a genuine puzzle: momentum and mean-reversion sound like they contradict each other, and they don't.

body.text: Value, momentum, and mean-reversion are three of the most well-documented factors in equity markets. Momentum and mean-reversion can coexist without contradiction because they operate at genuinely different time horizons, not because one of them is wrong.

children.text: The value factor ranks stocks by how cheap they are relative to some measure of their underlying fundamentals, then goes long the cheapest names and short the most expensive ones, or simply avoids the expensive ones in a long-only context. Screener.in, already used in this course for sector screening, is built almost entirely around exactly these metrics, making it a practical starting point for building a basic value ranking of NSE stocks.

cells: Price paid per rupee of annual earnings; lower is often considered cheaper
Price paid per rupee of net asset value; especially used for banks and financials
Enterprise value per rupee of operating earnings, capital-structure-neutral, useful across companies with different debt levels
Annual dividend per share divided by price; higher can indicate value, or can flag a struggling business, so it is used alongside other metrics

children.text: The momentum factor ranks stocks by their own recent trailing return, typically the past 6 to 12 months, and bets that recent winners keep winning and recent losers keep losing over the following few months, a well-documented pattern across many markets, including India. A common, more careful construction skips the most recent month: a 12-month return that excludes the last 30 days, since very short-term returns tend to behave more like the reversal Lesson 3 described than like the momentum effect being targeted.

body.label: The "12-1" momentum convention
body.value: 12-month trailing return, excluding the most recent 1 month
body.context: A standard construction in momentum research and practice, designed specifically to avoid contaminating a medium-term momentum signal with short-term reversal effects.

children.text: The Mean-Reversion Factor (What This Course Has Been Building)

This course has spent seven chapters building one specific member of the mean-reversion family: a relative-value signal that scores how stretched a pair's spread is relative to its own recent history, using the z-score from Lesson 7. It shares its basic logic, score a deviation, act on the extremes, with the broader mean-reversion factor family, just applied at the level of a single relationship rather than an entire universe.
The Apparent Contradiction: Winners Keep Winning vs Stretched Things Snap Back

Put momentum and mean-reversion side by side and they sound like they cannot both be true. Momentum says a stock that has recently done well tends to keep doing well. Mean-reversion says a price that has stretched away from its usual level tends to snap back. Both are genuinely, repeatedly documented in real market data. The resolution is not that one of them is wrong.
The resolution is time horizon. Depending on how far out you look, markets have shown a fairly consistent pattern across many studies and many markets.

body.caption: Documented return patterns across horizons (a widely discussed pattern in academic finance)

cells: Short-term reversal: sharp moves tend to partially revert
Yes, exactly the pairs and stat arb reversion this course has built
Momentum: recent winners tend to keep outperforming, recent losers keep underperforming
No, a different, medium-horizon factor family
Long-term reversal: extreme multi-year winners and losers tend to partially reverse
No, a much longer horizon, closer to value investing's territory

children.text: Days to weeks is exactly this course's territory, the half-life Lesson 3 introduced, and the entry and exit rules Lesson 14 built, all operate in that short-horizon reversal window. A 12-month momentum factor is measuring something genuinely different, a medium-horizon continuation effect, over a time frame this course's pairs trades are never held for.
Why They Don't Actually Contradict Each Other

A commonly proposed explanation, not a settled, universally agreed fact, is that these patterns come from different underlying causes. Short-term reversal is often attributed to overreaction and temporary liquidity effects that fade quickly. Medium-term momentum is often attributed to information about a company diffusing into the price gradually rather than all at once. Long-term reversal is often attributed to valuations eventually overshooting and correcting back toward fundamentals over several years. Different causes operating over different time frames is exactly why a trader can reasonably believe in short-term mean-reversion, this course's territory, without that belief contradicting a separate, medium-horizon momentum strategy.

body.title: Why don't momentum and mean-reversion contradict each other?
body.question: Momentum research suggests recent winners keep winning over the medium term. Mean-reversion research, the basis of this entire course, suggests stretched deviations tend to snap back. How can both be true?
options: Only one of them can actually be true; the other must be a statistical artifact
They operate over meaningfully different time horizons; short-term reversal (days to weeks) and medium-term momentum (roughly 3 to 12 months) are different, separately documented patterns
Momentum only applies to bonds, not stocks
Mean-reversion only applies to pairs, never to a single stock's own price history
body.explanation: The apparent contradiction dissolves once time horizon is accounted for. Short-term reversal (this course's territory, days to weeks) and medium-term momentum (roughly 3 to 12 months) are separately documented patterns operating over different windows, not competing claims about the same thing.

body.title: Which factor is this, really?
body.scenario: An analyst builds a signal ranking Nifty 500 stocks by their trailing 11-month return, deliberately excluding the most recent month's return from the calculation.
body.prompt: Which factor family does this signal belong to, and why was the most recent month specifically excluded?
body.modelAnswer: This is a momentum factor, using the standard "12-1" style construction (trailing return excluding the most recent month). The most recent month is excluded because very short-term returns tend to behave like the short-term reversal pattern this course's mean-reversion strategy targets, not like the medium-term continuation effect the momentum factor is actually trying to capture. Mixing the two in the same signal would blur two genuinely different, separately documented patterns.

body.title: Value, Momentum, and Horizon: Core Terms

cards.definition: A factor that ranks stocks by how cheap they are relative to fundamentals (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, dividend yield), typically going long the cheapest and short, or avoiding, the most expensive.

A factor that ranks stocks by their trailing return over roughly 6 to 12 months, betting that recent relative winners keep outperforming and recent losers keep underperforming over the following months.
The tendency for sharp, recent price moves, over days to a few weeks, to partially revert, the time horizon this course's mean-reversion strategies operate in.
The tendency for extreme multi-year winners and losers to partially reverse over a roughly 3 to 5 year horizon, a separate, much longer-horizon pattern from both momentum and short-term reversal.

points: The value factor ranks stocks by cheapness relative to fundamentals (P/E, P/B, EV/EBITDA, dividend yield); screener.in is a practical, familiar tool for building this kind of ranking on NSE stocks.
The momentum factor ranks stocks by trailing return, commonly over 12 months excluding the most recent month, betting recent relative winners keep outperforming over the following months.

Momentum and mean-reversion sound contradictory but are not: they are separately documented patterns operating over genuinely different time horizons, short-term reversal (days to weeks, this course's territory), medium-term momentum (roughly 3 to 12 months), and long-term reversal (roughly 3 to 5 years).

Commonly proposed explanations attribute these patterns to different underlying causes at each horizon: overreaction and liquidity effects short-term, gradual information diffusion medium-term, and valuation overshoot correcting over the long term.

Understanding these distinctions matters directly for combining factors, the subject of the next lesson, since carelessly blending signals from different horizons can blur what each one is actually supposed to be capturing.
